per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid, the general eligibility criteria for **CAP/DA services** are that the person must be a Medicaid beneficiary and must meet both the policy’s general coverage standards and CAP/DA-specific waiver criteria. In short:

## General CAP/DA eligibility

A beneficiary must:

- **Be enrolled in NC Medicaid.**
- **Not have an eligibility-category restriction that makes them ineligible for CAP/DA.**
- Meet the general Medicaid coverage standards that the service be:
  - **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the person’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis,
  - **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs,**
  - able to be **safely furnished,**
  - not replace an **equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment** available statewide, and
  - **not primarily for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) §§ 2.1.1, 3.1 (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current per amendment check)

## CAP/DA-specific criteria

NC Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary also:

- **Meets the required HCBS nursing facility level of care (LOC)** as determined by NC Medicaid;
- **Requires long-term care support** at a level typically provided in an institution, tied to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need;
- Has a completed **CAP assessment** showing a **reasonable indication** that the person will need at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within **30 calendar days** of evaluation;
- Has a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services on a monthly basis to help prevent institutionalization;
- Or, for certain short-term equipment/modification/technology needs, has a signed service plan authorizing those supports so the person can return to or remain in a **primary private residence** and avoid institutional placement;
- Can **maintain health, safety, and well-being** in the primary private residence or other approved location with formal and informal supports;
- Has paid care needs that can be maintained **within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver;
- Has a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate medical services; and
- Has an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** for times when caregivers or direct care staff are unavailable.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.2.1 (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current per amendment check)

## Age / program scope

The text surfaced for this question also indicates CAP/DA case-management entity requirements include experience serving **adults 18 years of age and older** with medical complexities or physical disabilities, which is consistent with CAP/DA being an adult waiver program.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 6.4.1 (effective Sept. 1, 2025; current per amendment check)

## Bottom line

A person is generally eligible for CAP/DA if they are an **NC Medicaid beneficiary** and, beyond ordinary Medicaid coverage rules, they qualify for the **CAP/DA waiver level of care and service-plan requirements** showing they need community-based long-term supports to avoid institutionalization.

If you want, I can also turn this into a shorter **screening checklist** for advocates or explain the difference between **general eligibility** and **reasons CAP/DA may be denied or terminated**.

per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid’s **Orthotics & Prosthetics** policy, the main **specifically not covered** items are certain categories of devices/supplies, and coverage generally requires that the item be ordered, medically necessary, and tied to the beneficiary’s condition and function.

## Specifically not covered

NC Medicaid does **not** cover the following under this policy:

### Item-specific exclusions
- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup or duplicate devices** kept on hand or available in different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**  
Cite: § 4.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

### General not-covered rules
A procedure, product, or service is also not covered if:
- the beneficiary does **not** meet the **eligibility requirements in Section 2.0**
- the beneficiary does **not** meet the **coverage criteria in Section 3.0**
- it **duplicates another provider’s** procedure, product, or service
- it is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**  
Cite: § 4.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

For coverage, the policy says orthotic or prosthetic items must meet these baseline requirements:

- They must be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- They must be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s **medical, physical, or functional level**
- They must be **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place
- There must be a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary and the ordering physician, PA, or NP **within 6 months before** the initiation of the orthotic/prosthetic
- The beneficiary’s need for the item must be **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering physician, PA, or NP  
Cite: § 3.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

### Additional medical-necessity standards
The policy further states:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when required to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary as a **replacement for all or part of the function** of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part, and the beneficiary must require the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**
- Orthotic and prosthetic devices must be:
  - a **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the beneficiary’s treatment plan
  - **consistent with the beneficiary’s diagnosis and medical condition**, especially functional limitations and symptoms
  - of **high quality**, with **replacement parts available and obtainable**  
Cite: § 3.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

NC Medicaid generally covers orthotics and prosthetics only when they are **ordered by an authorized clinician, medically necessary, functionally appropriate, recently evaluated face-to-face, and reviewed annually**. It specifically excludes items that are for **comfort/convenience, backup duplicates, nursing-facility residents, covered by another agency, or tied to hospice care**, and it also excludes duplicative or experimental/investigational items.  
Cites: § 3.2.1, § 4.1, § 4.2.1, [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

I checked amendments for Policy 5B and the retrieved record identifies **Orthotics & Prosthetics** as the current authoritative document, with no direct amendments returned.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services, the policy does set specific **entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria**.

## Criteria

### Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets the entrance criteria when the following are present:

- A current **DSM-5 diagnosis** (or subsequent edition);
- Behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and **functional impairment** consistent with that diagnosis;
- If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary refuses it, **outpatient services may still be provided** until the higher level is available or to support the beneficiary in engaging in that higher level of care;
- The beneficiary is **capable of developing skills** to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to treatment; and
- There is **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective** under North Carolina community practice standards.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) (effective 2025-04-15; current per amendment check).

### Continued service criteria
For continued outpatient behavioral health services, the policy requires:

- **Any one** of the following:
  - The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
  - The beneficiary remains **at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
  - The functional gains are **tenuous**;

**And, in addition, any one** of the following:
- The beneficiary has met current treatment plan goals, but **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; or
- The beneficiary is making **satisfactory progress** toward treatment goals and the documentation supports that.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.2, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) (effective 2025-04-15; current per amendment check).

### Discharge criteria
Discharge is appropriate when:

- The beneficiary’s level of functioning has **improved in relation to the treatment plan goals**;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wants the services**; or
- The beneficiary has not improved despite treatment-plan modifications and instead **needs a more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.3, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) (effective 2025-04-15; current per amendment check).

## Documentation note
The provider record must include **documentation of entrance criteria, continued service criteria, and discharge criteria**.  
Cite: § 7.3.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) (effective 2025-04-15; current per amendment check).

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For **beneficiaries under age 21**, the **EPSDT special provision can expand coverage of outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition**. But **EPSDT does not waive prior approval requirements**. If the therapy service requires prior approval, the child’s age alone does not eliminate that requirement. Clinical Coverage Policy 10A also states that EPSDT does **not** require coverage of services that are **unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, not medical in nature, or not generally recognized as accepted medical practice**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current; see § 2.2.1 and “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”)

## How EPSDT affects outpatient therapy coverage

In practical terms, for outpatient specialized therapies under Policy 10A:

- A child under 21 may receive coverage under the **EPSDT exception to policy limitations** if the service is medically necessary for the child’s condition. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1)
- However, **prior approval still applies when the service normally requires it**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”)
- For children, the policy also includes **under-21 medical-necessity visit guidelines** for speech-language and audiology therapy, tied to severity of impairment and limited to medically necessary visits within an authorization period not exceeding six calendar months. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 5.4)

## Therapy-specific standards for beneficiaries under 21

For example, Policy 10A includes pediatric criteria within the discipline sections:

- **Speech-language therapy** requires documented findings supporting medical necessity; for dysphagia, the findings must address listed deficits and be shown through a VFSE/MBS, FEES, or clinical feeding/swallowing evaluation. The section also includes age-specific criteria for beneficiaries from birth through age 20. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3)
- **Audiology therapy (aural rehabilitation)** is covered when the beneficiary demonstrates qualifying hearing loss or impaired auditory processing, with specified functional deficits and evaluation requirements. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.4)

So, EPSDT helps a child get coverage **despite ordinary limitations**, but the provider still has to show the therapy is medically necessary under the discipline-specific criteria, and prior approval rules still remain in place where required.

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

Policy 10A’s **Ordering Practitioners** section identifies the practitioners who may order services under this policy:

- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP)

([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.1.2)

Based on the text I could verify, those are the ordering practitioner types recognized in Policy 10A. I **could not verify from the retrieved sections that a different ordering-practitioner rule applies specifically only to beneficiaries under 21**; the under-21 distinctions I found were about **coverage/EPSDT and medical-necessity standards**, not a separate pediatric-only list of ordering professionals.

## Bottom line

- **EPSDT can broaden coverage** for medically necessary outpatient therapy services for Medicaid beneficiaries under 21.
- **EPSDT does not remove prior approval requirements** when prior approval is otherwise required.
- **The service still must meet medical-necessity standards**, and the policy excludes unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, non-medical, or non-accepted treatments.
- Orders under Policy 10A may come from **MDs, DOs, DPMs, CNMs, PAs, and NPs**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), current effective 2025-02-01)

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — **NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for a beneficiary who lives in an assisted living facility**, if the beneficiary meets the congregate-setting PCS eligibility criteria.

Under NC Medicaid’s congregate-setting PCS policy, coverage applies to a person who resides in **“a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)”** or certain other licensed group settings, and who also meets the required functional and medical criteria. The policy requires unmet needs in qualifying ADLs and other conditions such as medical stability and no other payer being responsible for the service. See **§ 3.2.1** of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment) (current authoritative document per amendment check).

Covered PCS in that setting includes hands-on help with qualifying ADLs and certain related supports, such as cueing, prompting, related IADLs, medication assistance tied to the condition, and certain device or delegated-task assistance. See **§ 3.3** of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

But **not everything associated with assisted living is covered**. NC Medicaid specifically excludes several services, including **“Room and Board.”** It also excludes items like transportation, errands, companion sitting/leisure activities, and ongoing supervision/monitoring. See **§ 4.2.1.2** of [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## Bottom line
- **Yes, PCS may be covered in an assisted living/adult care home setting**
- **Only for eligible beneficiaries who meet the policy criteria**
- **Room and board at the assisted living facility is not covered by PCS**

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under HCWD, there is **not a maximum total earned-income limit** in the surfaced policy text. The rule shown is that the **only income limit is a 150% FPL cap on unearned income**, while total countable income above that level affects fees and premiums rather than categorical eligibility. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

## HCWD income limit rule

MA-2180 says an applicant must “**meet the income requirements for his coverage group**,” and the HCWD income section states:

- “**Those who have unearned incomes greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible for HCWD.**”
- “Those whose total countable income is equal to or less than 150% of FPL have no cost sharing (other than applicable co-payments).”
- “Those whose total countable income is greater than 150% of FPL must pay a **$50 annual enrollment fee**.”
- “Those whose total countable monthly income exceeds 200% of FPL must pay a **monthly premium** in addition to the enrollment fee.”
- The premium “**increases as income increases until countable income exceeds 450% of FPL, at which point** these individuals must pay a **full premium**.” [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

The 2014 change notice also says HCWD was revised “**to remove limits on countable income except for the 150% of Federal Poverty Level (FPL) cap on unearned income**” and that “the only income limit for the HCWD program is the **150% FPL limit on unearned income**.” [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

## Premiums and fees

From the surfaced MA-2180 text:

- **At or below 150% FPL total countable income:** no cost sharing other than applicable co-pays. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- **Above 150% FPL total countable income:** **$50 annual enrollment fee**. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- **Above 200% FPL total countable monthly income:** monthly premium **plus** the $50 annual enrollment fee. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- **Above 450% FPL:** **full premium** (the 2014 change notice describes this as a “100% premium”). [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

## Current premium chart amounts

I could not verify current dollar premium amounts from the surfaced evidence as current, because MA-2180’s premium chart has been amended and the amendment history shows the **authoritative document is now** [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf), which specifically says: “**MA-2180.IV.I - HCWD Premiums Income chart has been updated.**”

So, based on the verified text here:

- **No maximum total earned-income limit was verified.**
- The verified eligibility cap is **unearned income over 150% FPL**.
- The verified cost-sharing structure is:
  - **≤150% FPL total countable income:** no premium
  - **>150% FPL:** **$50 annual enrollment fee**
  - **>200% FPL:** monthly premium + $50 annual enrollment fee
  - **>450% FPL:** full premium

If you want, I can next pull the **2025 HCWD premium chart** so I can give you the current monthly dollar amounts by income band.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a Medicaid-eligible nursing facility resident, subject to specific conditions. No more than **15 consecutive therapeutic leave days** may be taken **without NC Medicaid approval**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective 2024-08-07]

## Conditions that must be met

The policy says therapeutic leave is allowed only if:

- the person is a **Medicaid-eligible resident** occupying a nursing facility bed **for which NC Medicaid is paying reimbursement**;
- the leave is **for therapeutic purposes only**;
- the leave is **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**;
- the **necessity for the leave is documented in the resident’s plan of care**; and
- the **therapeutic justification for each instance** of leave is entered in the **resident’s health record**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Additional limits and rules

- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during approved therapeutic leave. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- The facility is paid its **full current Medicaid bed rate** for a bed reserved due to therapeutic leave, but **not** for days that **exceed the legal limit**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- Therapeutic leave is **not available** when the absence is for the purpose of receiving **inpatient or nursing services elsewhere**, or at a **different level of care in the current facility**, when those services are **paid for by Medicaid**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]
- Transportation from the facility to the therapeutic leave site is **not considered an emergency**, so **ambulance service is not reimbursed by Medicaid** for that purpose. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Bottom line

**60 days per calendar year**, with **physician-ordered, therapeutically justified leave**, documented in the **plan of care and health record**, and **more than 15 consecutive days requires NC Medicaid approval**. The current authoritative NC policy I checked is **Clinical Coverage Policy 2B-1, Nursing Facilities, effective August 7, 2024**, and I found no listed amendments overriding it.

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A PDN provider that ends services must notify **NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and the exact submission depends on why services are ending.

## NC Medicaid PDN policy requirements

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**, which appears current in the amendment record I checked:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to NC Medicaid **within 5 business days**.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary because another source of nursing coverage is available:**  
  The provider must, **within 5 business days**:
  - notify NC Medicaid, and
  - submit the **DMA-3513**.  
  The notice must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided and can be billed to Medicaid**, and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The PDN provider must provide NC Medicaid, **within 5 business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order to terminate PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513**.

- **If services end because the beneficiary loses NC Medicaid eligibility, or no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days (including hospitalization):**  
  The policy says the **prior approval process must be initiated again** under Subsections 5.1 and 5.2 before PDN resumes. This is a reauthorization consequence rather than a separate notice form requirement. [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

## Appeal / notice distinction

The same PDN section states that when the **attending physician and/or the PDN service provider** decides to discharge the beneficiary, **that decision cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid**. By contrast, if **NC Medicaid** terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, **NC Medicaid (or its designee) must give the beneficiary/legal representative written notice of the adverse decision, including appeal rights**. [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

If the beneficiary is in **managed care**, federal rules also require written notice of an adverse benefit determination and set content requirements for that notice, including reasons, appeal rights, and continuation-of-benefits information. See **§ 438.404** and **§ 438.210(c)** of **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**.

## Bottom line

For a provider-initiated PDN termination, the core NC Medicaid rule is:

- **Submit DMA-3513 to NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and
- if applicable, also send:
  - **notice of other coverage** with the last billable date and coverage source, or
  - the **physician’s termination order**.

If you want, I can also pull together this into a short **practice checklist** for providers or advocates.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner order and written plan-of-care rules. The regulation defines the covered home health service categories as:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis;
- **Home health aide services**;
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in settings where normal life activities take place; and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services** (this therapy category is optional for states).  
  Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70.

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided **“at [the beneficiary’s] place of residence.”** But the regulation also explains what counts and what does **not** count as a place of residence for this purpose.

### Included settings
A beneficiary may receive home health services in **any setting in which normal life activities take place**, and the services **cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1).

### Excluded settings
For home health services, a beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

**except** that some home health services may be provided in an ICF/IID if those services are **not required to be provided by the facility** itself.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c).

The regulation also says home health services may not be provided in **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1).

## Core conditions attached to the definition

For federal Medicaid home health services, the regulation requires:

- an order written by a **physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant**, acting in accordance with state law, for services described in § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4);
- a **written plan of care**; and
- **review by the ordering practitioner every 60 days** for those services.

For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances under § 440.70(b)(3), the rule uses slightly different ordering language and says the plan of care must be reviewed as specified in that paragraph.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a).

## Bottom line

Federal law defines Medicaid home health services as certain nursing, aide, supply/equipment, and therapy services furnished under required orders and a written plan of care, and they must be provided **at the beneficiary’s residence or another setting where normal life activities occur—not in institutional inpatient settings like hospitals or nursing facilities**.  
Current federal authority: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice, a person is treated as **terminally ill** when the required certification supports a **life expectancy of six months or less** if the illness runs its normal course. NC Medicaid’s hospice certification rules repeatedly use that standard, including requiring later recertifications to explain why face-to-face clinical findings support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), § 5.4.1; D. “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within **two calendar days after the period begins**, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two days, and the written certification must still be obtained before the claim is submitted. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1.

### Who must sign it
- **Initial 90-day benefit period:** certification is required from  
  - the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; **and**
  - the beneficiary’s **attending physician**, if the beneficiary has one.  
  [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

- **Subsequent benefit periods:** only the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice IDG** must certify.  
  [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

## What the certification/recertification must contain

The certification or recertification must include:
- a physician narrative that **briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis** and attests the physician composed it after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- the **election period dates** to which it applies; and
- the physician’s **signature and date**.  
  [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), D. “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

For the **third benefit period recertification and every recertification after that**, a **face-to-face encounter** by a hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner must occur **before, but no more than 30 calendar days before**, the recertification, to gather clinical findings on continued eligibility. The related narrative must explain why those findings support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1; D. “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

## Timing rules
- Initial certifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- Recertifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the start of the next benefit period.  
  [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1; D. “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

I checked amendments for Policy 3D, and the tool returned **no amendments**, with **Hospice Services (effective Mar. 15, 2024)** as the authoritative current document.

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Speech therapy may be provided by telehealth under NC Medicaid **only for a select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions**, and only when telehealth is **medically necessary** under the policy’s telehealth conditions. In particular:

- Telehealth may be medically necessary if the beneficiary’s **medical condition makes exposure to others something that should be avoided**, or if the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** with limited access to appropriately qualified providers.
- **Unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable**, telehealth must be used **as an adjunct to in-person care, not as a replacement**.
- Telehealth must be used **in the beneficiary’s best interest**, **not for the therapist’s convenience**.
- Telehealth may **never** be used **solely to increase therapist productivity**.  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current per amendment check, section “e. Telehealth”)

In addition, the **ordinary Medicaid speech-language therapy medical-necessity rules still apply**. So telehealth does not create separate coverage for speech therapy; the beneficiary still has to meet the policy’s regular speech-language therapy criteria for the service being provided. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01, current per amendment check, § 3.2.1.3 “Speech-Language Therapy (ST)”)

## Bottom line
NC Medicaid allows speech therapy via telehealth when it is a covered speech/language service and telehealth is medically necessary for the beneficiary, especially because exposure should be avoided or access is limited due to a remote/underserved location. But telehealth generally must remain **supplemental to in-person care** unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable, and it cannot be used for provider convenience or productivity.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care plans do **not automatically have to meet a universal 85% MLR floor**. Instead, the federal rule requires states to make each Medicaid MCO/PIHP/PAHP **calculate and report** MLR, and **if** a state chooses to impose a minimum MLR, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. North Carolina goes further: its PHP contract sets a **minimum MLR threshold of 88% in aggregate across all contracted PHPs**, with plan-specific thresholds based on capitation-revenue mix. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)] [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

## Federal rule

### 1) What federal law requires
Federal Medicaid managed care rules require the state, through its contracts, to ensure that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR for each reporting year. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

The key threshold rule is conditional:

- **If a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85%**. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

So the federal rule is:

- **Mandatory calculation/reporting** for Medicaid managed care plans; and
- **Optional minimum threshold**, but if imposed by the state, it must be **at least 85%**. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

### 2) How federal MLR is calculated
Federal law defines MLR as:

- **Numerator / Denominator**, with a possible **credibility adjustment** for partially credible plans. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

At a high level:

**Numerator**
- incurred claims,
- expenditures for activities that improve health care quality, and
- fraud prevention activities. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

**Denominator**
- adjusted premium revenue, with taxes and licensing/regulatory fees treated as specified in the federal rule. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

The rule also specifies inclusions/exclusions, such as:
- including certain provider incentive/bonus payments tied to clinical or quality standards,
- including state directed payments described in the rule,
- deducting overpayment recoveries and prescription drug rebates from incurred claims, and
- excluding non-claims administrative costs from incurred claims. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

### 3) Federal oversight if a state uses a minimum MLR
If a state requires a minimum MLR, the state must annually report to CMS, for each managed care plan, at least:

- numerator amount,
- denominator amount,
- MLR percentage achieved,
- member months, and
- any remittances owed. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

If the state requires remittances for failure to meet the state minimum MLR, the state must also reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance and separately report the methodology for the state/federal share calculation. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina implements the federal rule in its PHP contract by requiring each PHP to:

- calculate and report **CMS-defined MLR** annually, aligned to the rating year and defined by **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**;
- also calculate a separate **Department-defined MLR**;
- use federal-style numerator and denominator rules, with state-specific adjustments; and
- make a payment or approved contribution if its Department-defined MLR falls below the state minimum threshold. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### NC’s threshold
The NC contract states:

- “The minimum MLR threshold in aggregate across all contracted PHPs shall be exactly **88%**...” [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

It further says a PHP’s own threshold is calculated based on the plan’s **capitation revenue mix**, using a revenue-weighted approach across rate cells. The retrieved text is truncated before the full formula, so I can confirm the weighted-threshold concept but not the complete formula from the excerpt retrieved. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### NC’s CMS-defined MLR
NC requires the PHP to calculate the **CMS-defined MLR** exactly under the federal framework:

- numerator = incurred claims + expenditures for activities that improve health care quality + the lesser of fraud reduction expenditures or fraud reduction recoveries, as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(e);
- denominator = premium revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees, as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(f). [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### NC’s Department-defined MLR adjustments
NC also creates a **Department-defined MLR**, similar to the federal MLR but with additional state-specific adjustments. The contract says:

**Allowed additions**
- PHPs may include certain voluntary contributions to health-related resources if they align with the Department’s Quality Strategy, reflect meaningful community engagement, are non-discriminatory across members and NC regions, and are spent directly on improving beneficiary outcomes such as housing, meals, transportation, or other essential services. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

**Required exclusions**
- required additional directed payments reimbursed separately by the Department,
- payments to related providers that violate contract payment limitations,
- interest/penalty payments for prompt-pay failures,
- certain rebates or prior-year substitution contributions,
- non-claims costs, PBM fees and spread pricing, marketing/branding material, related-party administrative payments and margin, and administrative costs not allowed as health care quality improvement. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

**Denominator adjustment**
- Department reimbursements for required additional directed payments to providers are subtracted from the denominator, along with associated taxes and fees. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### Credibility adjustment and consequences
NC’s contract also says:

- PHPs with fewer than **380,000 member months** in an MLR reporting year must use a credibility adjustment defined by 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(h)(1)-(3). [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

If a PHP’s **Department-defined MLR** is below the minimum threshold, the contract requires the PHP to do one of the following:

- remit a rebate to the Department,
- make approved contributions to health-related resources, or
- split the obligation between the two. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** Medicaid managed care plans must **calculate and report** MLR; a state-imposed minimum MLR is optional, but if adopted it must be **at least 85%**. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]
- **North Carolina:** NC implements that rule through PHP contract requirements and sets an **88% aggregate minimum MLR threshold** across contracted PHPs, with plan-specific thresholds based on revenue mix, plus state-specific rules for rebates/contributions and what counts in the Department-defined MLR. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the policy’s general medical-necessity standards **and** the therapy meets the policy’s CAR-T-specific requirements.

## Coverage criteria

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, effective April 1, 2025**, CAR-T cell therapy is covered if:

### 1) General coverage criteria are met
The service must be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs;
- safely furnished, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide; and
- furnished in a manner not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider.  
  [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1]

### 2) CAR-T-specific criteria are met
The policy specifically requires that:

- **the CAR-T therapy has received U.S. FDA approval;**
- **the therapy is administered according to U.S. FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions; and
- **the therapy is administered at a certified or authorized treatment center.** If the therapy is subject to an FDA-required **REMS** program, the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS program, and providers must be trained to manage **cytokine release syndrome (CRS)** and **neurologic toxicities**.  
  [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.2.1]

## Practical limits / when it is not covered
The same policy says CAR-T is **not covered** if, among other things:

- the product is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is administered **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy that requires REMS is administered at a facility **not enrolled** in that REMS program;
- it is **repeat treatment** in a beneficiary who previously received another CAR-T therapy;
- the beneficiary’s psychosocial history limits ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- there is current beneficiary or caregiver noncompliance making adherence to the medical regimen improbable.  
  [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.2.1]

The policy also generally excludes services if the beneficiary does not meet Section 3 criteria, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.  
[[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.1]

## Documentation typically required for approval
For prior approval, the policy calls for documentation including:

- a physician-signed letter of medical necessity documenting prior chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical and social history, and indications for CAR-T;
- verification that the administering facility is a qualified/authorized treatment center;
- recent HIV and hepatitis serologies;
- diagnostic and procedure results, including bone marrow biopsy (not more than six months old); and
- a complete psychological and social evaluation addressing compliance, support network, post-treatment care plan, and relevant mental health, substance use, or legal history.  
  [[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2]

## Bottom line
The key NC Medicaid rule is: **CAR-T is covered only for an FDA-approved CAR-T product, used exactly within FDA-approved parameters, and administered at a properly certified/authorized center, with REMS compliance when required.** General medical-necessity standards also apply.  
[[CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), §§ 3.1, 3.2.1]

I also checked amendments for Policy **11A-17** and the authoritative current document is the **April 1, 2025** version.

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than the participant’s individual base budget if the participant believes their needs cannot be met within that budget. NC Medicaid’s policy says the SIS results and base budget are only guidelines, not a binding cap on what may be requested or authorized. If the LME/MCO determines the services are medically necessary, they must be authorized even if they exceed the base budget. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), effective Nov. 1, 2016, current authoritative document, “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes”)

If the participant believes the budget is insufficient, the policy indicates two key protections:

- **They can still ask for more services above the base budget** based on unmet need.  
- **If the request is denied**, the LME/MCO must tell the participant the reasons for the denial and **how to appeal**. The policy also references **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), effective Nov. 1, 2016, current authoritative document, “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes”)

For some high-intensity service requests, the policy also shows that approvals can be time-limited and revisited based on **medical necessity**. For example, requests for more than 16 hours daily are authorized for up to a 90-day period within the plan year, and any extension beyond that requires medical-necessity review. The treatment team should then review the person’s status, identify sustainable supports, and consider both waiver and non-waiver options, including Medicaid State Plan services. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), effective Nov. 1, 2016, current authoritative document, “NC Medicaid North Carolina Innovations”)

## Bottom line
A participant is **not limited to the base budget** if their actual needs are greater. They can request services above that amount, and if the LME/MCO says no, the participant should receive notice of the reasons and appeal rights, and may also pursue a grievance about the base budget.
